title: Fenwae, Silver Star Stone Mason
type: Silver Star mason and quarry guide
dek: A Silver Star mason whose work on drinking water and a teacher’s memorial becomes a patient conversation about discipline, belonging and the possibility of changing one’s mind.

body:
Fenwae is a mason of the Silver Star who shows Olokun the work beneath Zarathis’s beauty. Stone, water, bodily discipline and a teacher’s memory give them common ground. Their conversation also makes room for disagreement about Aria and how outsiders have been treated.

An honest invitation

During the Zarathian cultural visit on 11, Month of Moirah, Year 2, Fenwae offers Olokun a trip to the mines. He does not promise courtly splendor. The work may not be pretty, he says, but it is honest. Olokun accepts an introduction to the labor beneath the city’s wealth.

Fenwae is a Silver Star stone mason and a practical host. He makes room for a visitor to ask questions and offer help, rather than presenting the culture only through its most powerful people.

Good stone and drinking water

Teleportation circles carry the visitors to a mountain mine. Fenwae explains that gold, silver and gems are not the whole purpose of the place: sound building stone matters. He values marble as the foundation of architecture and the work of a society that must keep making things.

He is helping dam a mountain lake to gather clean drinking water. When Olokun offers his experience with water, Fenwae shows him the project and says that the work is discussed with the Verdant Circle. Their assurance that a restored trickle will let the ecosystem recover remains a reported assessment, not a completed ecological survey.

He enjoys the effort itself. Selecting the right stone with a pickaxe and feeling the strength in his arms appeal to him more than a grand claim to artistic genius. Fine carving is a welcome change, but he knows what part of the work he most loves.

The marble for a teacher’s memory

Fenwae helped select a block of marble for a memorial to Xo, a revered teacher. He shows Olokun an animated image of the work. He is careful about his own connection: he never had the honor of learning from Xo directly. The teacher’s extraordinary discipline and purity are things Fenwae has heard and admires.

What matters to him is how those teachings continue in ordinary work. He describes people carrying discipline into fishing, farming, carving and watching the stars. Care for the body and respect for oneself belong to everyone, not only to specialist fighters.

Olokun finds something familiar in that idea. They compare teachings about caring for oneself before helping others, and the conversation becomes more personal. Fenwae offers a proverb about knowing when to stand, kneel or crawl. The visitor’s response grows sadder; shared values do not remove what he is carrying.

A friend willing to reconsider

Fenwae wants Olokun to see a hardworking, balanced people, rather than monsters. Admiration for Aria shapes his account of the public dispute: he finds the questioning of a local hero painful and offensive.

Olokun answers that the visitors came to help and risked their lives, then felt betrayed when their motives were publicly doubted. Fenwae listens. He acknowledges that they experienced the same day differently and says Olokun has given him something to think about. His willingness to reconsider is a recorded response; his suggestion that truth may lie in the beholder’s eye does not settle the disputed history.

Their parting stays practical and generous. Olokun offers help with the dam or memorial. Fenwae says another pair of hands is welcome, along with company and a kind spirit.

Evidence and limits

Olokun sees the work Fenwae shows him and hears what the mason values. Xo’s extraordinary life and the expected recovery of the dammed waterway reach the reader through Fenwae’s account. Their conversation establishes the exchange without supplying a complete career.

The open record

The final condition of the dam, completion of the memorial, Fenwae’s later work and the reach of his authority remain unestablished. His testimony does not make every Zarathian share the same judgment, and his respect for Xo does not make him Xo’s direct disciple.

profile.personality: Shows Olokun the work behind Zarathian stonecraft, water engineering and a teacher’s memorial.
profile.achievements: Fenwae offers Olokun a mine visit, explains why good building stone matters and shows a mountain-lake dam project. He says the work is discussed with the Verdant Circle and describes choosing marble for a memorial to Xo. In their later exchange about Aria, Fenwae’s admiration and Olokun’s differing account remain attributed perspectives. His masonry, practical hospitality and willingness to keep talking are established without making his defense of Zarathian society objective fact.
